title: Security & Compliance Controlbook: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence & Exceptions
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Overview

This controlbook documents Redwood Inference's baseline security and compliance requirements across the following domains: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC controls, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence collection and storage workflows, and the process for risk acceptance and exceptions. The purpose is to centralize policy, operational steps, ownership, and minimal technical configurations so teams can implement controls consistently and demonstrably for audits.

Scope

Applies to: all Redwood-managed services, hosted control plane components, Dedicated and Private deployment delivery processes, and internal tools that access production data.

Not in scope: third-party SaaS applications where third-party contractual SLAs and controls apply (these require separate vendor risk assessments).

Definitions

- Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): Grant only the minimum privileges required for a role to perform its tasks.
- Control Owner: Person/team accountable for a specific control area (see Ownership section).
- Evidence Artifact: Any document, log, screenshot, config file or export used to demonstrate a control is in place.

Ownership and Escalation

- Security (owner): maintains policy, reviewers, control maturity and audit evidence retention.
- Eng-Infra: implements access controls at cloud, network, and infra layers.
- Eng-SRE: implements logging, monitoring, and retention SLOs.
- Product/Eng: implement SDLC and secure coding practices.
- Legal & Compliance: provides regulatory interpretation and accepts risk exceptions.

RBAC and Authentication

High-level requirements

1) Centralized identity: All human users must authenticate through the corporate identity provider (IdP: Okta). Service-to-service authentication uses short-lived mTLS or cloud-native workload identities (Workload Identity Federation).
2) Role taxonomy: Define and publish canonical roles (owner, admin, developer, readonly, auditor) for each service. Role definitions must include allowed actions and resource scopes.
3) PoLP enforcement: Default access is deny. Requests for elevated access use the access request workflow (see Exceptions). Temporary elevated access must be time-bound and auditable.
4) MFA: MFA is mandatory for all interactive logins with API or console access.
5) Secrets management: No long-lived secrets in source control. Use KMS (HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS) and rotate keys per key rotation schedule.

Operational controls and examples

- Okta groups must map 1:1 to IAM roles where supported (example: okta-group-eng-prod-admin -> aws:role/prod-admin).
- Service accounts: all non-human principals must be short-lived tokens (TTL <= 24h) or use workload identities.
- Privileged access reviews: quarterly reviews of all users with admin privileges; remediation tracked in the security ticket queue.

Audit logging

Requirements

- Capture: All authentication events (success/failure), authorization decisions for privileged APIs, configuration changes, and data access to regulated datasets must be captured.
- Integrity: Logs must be immutable after write (append-only store) and tagged with source, shard, and retention policy.
- Retention SLOs: Logs for critical systems retained 7 years; auth and admin logs retained 3 years; operational logs (non-regulated) retained 1 year unless project-specific exception approved.
- Availability SLO: Audit log ingestion pipeline SLA 99.9% monthly; alert on ingestion drop >5 minutes.

Implementation notes

- Collector: use the centralized audit-log-collector service that forwards to the audit lake (encrypted S3) and a real-time stream to SIEM (Splunk/Datadog).
- Metadata: every log must include principal_id, request_id, service, environment, resource, action, result, timestamp, and correlation_id.
- Access control: read access to raw logs is restricted to the auditor and security groups; SREs get scoped views via dashboards.

Example logging policy (pseudo-table)

| Log Type | Minimum Fields | Retention |
|---|---:|---:|
| Auth events | principal_id, ip, user_agent, result, timestamp | 3 years |
| Admin/config changes | principal_id, change_delta, before, after, timestamp | 7 years |
| Data access (regulated) | principal_id, dataset_id, object_id, access_method, timestamp | 7 years |

Data Residency and Retention

Policy summary

- Data residency decisions must be made at the dataset level and enforced via cloud region tagging and network controls.
- Redwood supports regional deployments for customers with residency requirements; production customer data is hosted only in permitted regions (e.g., us-east-1, eu-west-1) per contract.
- Retention baselines: customer-generated model inputs/outputs (short-lived, default 30 days), audit/evidence artifacts (per compliance schedule), backups and snapshots (90 days unless regulated).

Minimum technical controls

- Region locking: infra templates must include a required_region tag that enforces resource creation constraints.
- Encryption: data-at-rest encrypted with KMS; keys are region-scoped for customers who require regional keys.
- Data access labeling: datasets must include metadata for classification (public/internal/confidential/regulated). Access policies evaluate dataset classification and principal attributes.

Retention schedule (baseline)

- Regulated customer data: retain per contract; default 7 years for financial/health data when required.
- Model inference inputs/outputs: default 30 days (configurable per customer).
- Backups: 90 days; longer if required by customer contract.

Secure SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle)

Controls required for all production services

1) Threat modeling: New services and significant changes require threat model and documented mitigations before design sign-off.
2) Dependency policy: Approved package registries and dependency vulnerability scanning (automated SCA pipeline). Block builds on high/severe unmitigated CVEs.
3) Code review: All changes to production code require at least one approver from the owning team and one security reviewer for high-risk changes.
4) CI/CD hardening: Build artifacts signed; pipelines run in ephemeral workers; credential injection is via secrets manager at runtime.
5) Static and dynamic analysis: Static application security testing (SAST) on merge and DAST for public-facing endpoints on release candidate builds.

Secure release checklist (example)

- [ ] Threat model completed and approved
- [ ] SCA scan results reviewed
- [ ] SAST completed with no critical findings
- [ ] Release signed and artifact provenance recorded
- [ ] Rollback plan documented and smoke tests prepared

Incident Response — Security Procedures

Goals: detect, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn.

Team roles

- Incident Commander (IC): coordinates response and communications.
- Security Lead: drives technical investigation and containment.
- SRE Lead: implements containment in infra and monitors systems.
- Legal & Privacy: advises on regulatory/customer notification needs.
- Communications: drafts customer and internal communications.

Incident lifecycle (concise runbook)

1) Triage and severity classification: use severity matrix (S1: active data exfiltration/production outage affecting customers; S2: limited data exposure; S3: internal-only incident).
2) Containment: isolate affected services, rotate keys/credentials if compromise suspected, and apply immediate ACLs.
3) Evidence preservation: capture forensic snapshots, preserve relevant audit logs (mark retention to prevent deletion during investigation).
4) Root cause analysis and eradication: remove malicious artifacts, patch vulnerabilities.
5) Recovery: reintroduce services to traffic gradually with monitoring and canary checks.
6) Post-incident review: 72-hour interim report; 30-day postmortem with action items and owners.

Key detection and escalation triggers

- Unexpected spikes in data export rates from regulated datasets (threshold: >3x baseline for 10 minutes).
- Multiple failed privileged login attempts from foreign IPs over 15 minutes.
- Audit log ingestion gaps >5 minutes.

Compliance Evidence Workflows

What to collect

- Configuration snapshots (IAM policies, network ACLs, service configs).
- Audit log exports corresponding to control periods.
- Policy documents, runbooks, and approval artifacts (Jira tickets, design docs).
- Test evidence for automated controls (SCA/SAST reports, build provenance).

Storage and naming conventions

- Canonical storage: s3://redwood-compliance-evidence/<control-id>/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<artifact-type>-<owner>.tar.gz (encrypted at rest).
- Metadata: each artifact MUST have a metadata JSON sidecar (artifact_id, control_id, created_by, created_at, retention_until, description).
- Access: only Security and Compliance engineers have write access. Read access granted via IAM roles and ephemeral sessions for auditors.

Evidence retention and audit readiness

- Maintain an evidence index (single CSV/DB export) that maps controls to artifacts, owners, and retention.
- Periodic evidence collection: automated quarterly exports for high-risk controls; ad-hoc exports for audit requests within 3 business days.

Risk and Exceptions

Exception request process

1) Submit an exception request via the security exceptions form (Jira project: SEC-EXCEPTIONS) with the following fields: control_id, scope, requested_timeline, compensating_controls, business_justification, owner.
2) Security triage evaluates severity and recommends compensating controls.
3) For high-risk exceptions, present to the Risk Acceptance Board (Security + Legal + Business owner) for approval.
4) Approved exceptions must have an expiration date (<= 12 months) and an automated reminder to re-evaluate 30 days before expiry.

Compensating controls examples

- If RBAC cannot be immediately implemented, require session recording, Just-In-Time elevation, and increased monitoring for principals in scope.
- If retaining logs longer is infeasible, export summarized hashed digests to the compliance evidence store and document the limitation.

Risk register and metrics

- Maintain a risk register (table with id, description, owner, likelihood, impact, residual risk, mitigation plan) and review monthly in the security working group.
- Key metrics: number of open exceptions, average time to remediation, age of highest-risk exceptions.

Appendices

A. Quick-check controls mapping (example)

- Control: IAM provisioning and reviews -> Evidence: Okta group exports, quarterly review tickets -> Owner: Eng-Infra
- Control: Audit logging -> Evidence: audit-lake index, SIEM dashboards, retention config -> Owner: Eng-SRE
- Control: Secure SDLC -> Evidence: threat model docs, SAST reports, release checklist -> Owner: Product/Eng
